articles.title_orig: King, dingers power Padres in G1 rout at frenzied Petco
articles.title_zh: King, dingers power Padres in G1 rout at frenzied Petco
articles.content_orig:
SAN DIEGO -- They packed Petco Park anticipating a party in the Gaslamp on Tuesday night. The Cubs could do little to stop it. The Padres wouldn't let it end.
Three pitches into the top of the first inning, Michael King punched out Pete Crow-Armstrong. The ballpark erupted. Eight pitches later, King had retired the side in order. Louder, still. Leading off the bottom of the first, Fernando Tatis Jr. crushed the first pitch he saw over the center-field wall. Somehow, even louder.
That noise reached a crescendo two batters later, when Manny Machado launched another home run off Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd . The Padres were well on their way to an 8-0 victory in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series. The party in downtown San Diego never stopped.
“The crowd was great,” said Cubs manager Craig Counsell. “... They had a lot to cheer about tonight -- and we didn't give them anything to be quiet about.”
King would carry a no-hitter into the seventh. By the time Nico Hoerner broke up King’s bid at history with a soft single down the third-base line with one out in the seventh, the Padres had built a 7-0 lead. It was the longest individual postseason no-hit bid since Aníbal Sánchez went 7 2/3 for the Nationals in the 2019 NLCS. King would finish with seven innings of one-hit ball.
Postseason Guide • Final bracket • Wild Card Series matchups • How to watch Wild Card Series on NBC, Peacock • Postseason schedule
King would allow just that one hit over seven innings -- 28 years to the day that Kevin Brown punched out 16 Astros in the 1998 NLDS. That game is widely regarded as the greatest single-game pitching performance in franchise history. King made a strong case for No. 2.
The game stood in stark contrast to last year’s Wild Card Series between these two teams, which Chicago controlled throughout. Suddenly, the Cubs’ backs are against the wall. And the Padres are one win from a trip to Milwaukee and the NLDS.
“Obviously we've got to continue doing it,” Machado said. “Not all games are going to be like the one today. But we're always ready for the battle.”
Here are some takeaways from Game 1:
1. This is a very different Padres offense
Maybe a few of the names are the same. But this is not the Padres offense that scored all of five runs across three games in last year’s Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field.
For a month now, the Padres have been the best offense in baseball. And if there were any doubt whether that would carry over into October … the Padres erased it with a couple swings in the bottom of the first inning.
"We’re one. We’re coming together as one group," Tatis said. "At-bat after at-bat, we trust each other."
Tatis and Machado became the first Padres teammates to combine for multiple home runs in the first inning of a playoff game in franchise history. Xander Bogaerts would add a homer of his own in the fourth. The Padres poured it on.
By the fifth inning Tuesday night they’d scored more than they had in that entire three-game series at Wrigley Field a year ago.
“We did a good job with Tatis last year,” Counsell said. “We did not do a good job today, and it starts with that.”
Indeed, Tatis struggled last postseason -- and seemed to be at the center of everything on Tuesday night. But beyond that, the Padres offense is just … deeper this year. There are more levers to pull, and Stammen has been pulling them.
2. Boyd’s changeup betrays him
One of the keys to Boyd being as effective and consistent as he has been for the Cubs is the reliability of his changeup. It is his signature offspeed offering, but the lefty’s command of the pitch eluded him in Game 1 and it proved costly.
All three home runs surrendered by Boyd came off his changeup, marking the first time in his career (regular season or postseason) that he allowed that many homers in a game off that pitch. The blasts from Tatis, Machado and Bogaerts each came off changeups that were left in the strike zone.
“When it comes down to it, I just wasn’t as sharp with my changeup,” Boyd said. “It could have been better. They definitely could’ve been better. A team like that, especially Machado and Tatis, they’re going to be aggressive. I just didn’t throw it where I wanted to and they hit the mistakes.”
While allowing homers was an issue for the Cubs’ staff this season – their 231 homers surrendered led the NL – Boyd was one of the better performers on that front. In fact, the lefty allowed no homers in September, only two in his final seven starts combined and only allowed two or more in a game in three of his 22 starts.
3. Michael King might’ve done more than just win Game 1
The Padres have the sport's best bullpen. But how much stress could it handle across three games this week?
Well, now they really only need to worry about two -- at most.
Not only was King electric. The fact that he covered seven innings -- not to mention the tack-on runs from the Padres offense -- could go a long way toward helping them win the series. Mason Miller and Adrian Morejon are still fresh. The whole bullpen is, really.
The Cubs’ uphill climb in Games 2 and 3 just got a whole lot steeper. A red-hot Nick Pivetta gets the ball in Game 2 -- and Stammen can turn to his high-leverage arms whenever he needs to.
4. Cubs needed their lineup to step up
The Cubs ended the season leading the Major Leagues in runs scored (850), walks (674), slugging percentage (.428) and OPS (.767), while pacing the NL in home runs (220). A deep October run was going to be contingent on that offense continuing to roll, given the rocky nature of Chicago’s pitching.
Game 1 against the Padres could not have gone worse in that regard for the North Siders. The Cubs went 0-for-20 into the seventh inning before Hoerner’s infield single. Chicago’s dynamic one-two punch of Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman finished a combined 0-for-7 with six strikeouts.
“He was really good. Tip your cap,” Bregman said of King. “He threw the ball really well. Had everything really working and we didn’t do, really, anything right today. The good news is we get to show up tomorrow and play a baseball game. We’ve just got to execute better in all phases of the game.”

articles.title_orig: In Fractious France, Politicians Agree on One Thing: Pope Leo Was a Hit
articles.title_zh: In Fractious France, Politicians Agree on One Thing: Pope Leo Was a Hit
articles.content_orig:
By Isabella H. de Carvalho
The Cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris and "the tragedy it has enduredâ can âsymbolically shed light on this entire Apostolic Journeyâ to France, âoffering a perspective that I would summarize in one word: rebirth,â Pope Leo XIV said during the Wednesday General Audience in St. Peterâs Square on September 30.
Pope Leo XIV visited Paris, Lourdes and the northeastern city of Metz during his Apostolic Journey to France from September 25 to 28. During the visit he met thousands of young people in a stadium, emphasized the importance of defending life at all its stages, and appealed for peace in Europe and across the world.
On the first day of his Apostolic Journey, he celebrated Vespers in the Cathedral of Notre Dame in Paris, which was destroyed in April 2019 due to a fire and was then restored and reopened in December 2024.
In his catechesis, Pope Leo thanked all those who welcomed him and participated and emphasized how the rebirth of the Cathedral helps us to understand his whole Apostolic Journey and the fruits it could bring for the future.
Read the full text of the Pope's catechesis at the General Audience
The Pope underlined how the disaster of the fire at Notre-Dame and its subsequent rebuilding âsparked a positive reaction at every level,â such as for example the restoration process.
It was an example of collaboration âbetween the Church, the State, public institutions and civil society,â and helped make the most of âboth the generosity of benefactors and the expertise of professionals and skilled workers,â he explained.
This "synergy for the common good" should become "the norm for institutions, political and social forces, and all those with civil and economic responsibilities", Pope said. He explained that he conveyed this same message in his meeting with the French authorities and his address at UNESCO.
For the Pope âthe fundamental criterion upon which such collaboration must be basedâ is âthe dignity of the human person.â
Pope Leo also drew a parallel between the Vespers in Notre-Dame and the âunforgettableâ prayer vigil he participated in shortly after with 80,000 young people in the Stade de France stadium in Paris.
âTwo completely different locations," he explained, "yet two complementary events, almost united spiritually. What united them? The Church, which is not made up of stones or cement, but of people who love Jesus Christ because they have been loved by Him".
At the stadium there was the ânew French generation,â not 'new' so much because of their age but because of their âspiritâ and their âfreedom of heart and faith,â the Pope said.
There was singing and shouting but also silence and listening and âattentive and emotional faces, which revealed hearts yearning for truth and love,â the Pope continued, adding that âthe Vigil was a great sign of hope.â
For the Pope this same hope was manifested in his visit to Maison Bakhita, a welcome center for migrants, âwhere people commit themselves every day to serving the dignity of the human person with love.â
Another sign of renewal the Pope pointed to was the growing number of baptisms of young people and adults in France in recent years. During his visit he encouraged them by participating in a provincial synodal assembly underway in Paris, which is responding to âthis beautiful âsurpriseâ from God.â
Pope Leo then also recalled his Mass in the central Parisian square Place de la Concorde with around 700,000 people, who filled the iconic Avenue des Champs Élysées, up to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.
âAt the moment of Communion, everyone was able to receive the Eucharist, which was distributed everywhere," he said. "This is the true reconstruction, the restoration of the Church that only God can bring about, through the intercession of the Virgin Mary".
The Pope then turned to his âpilgrimageâ to Lourdes and its famous Marian shrine, âa sanctuary of the civilization of loveâ and the second leg of his Apostolic Journey.
âIn Lourdes, the Lord, through the maternal care of the Virgin Mary, conveys to everyone, pilgrims and especially those who are sick in body and spirit, a message of hope and rebirth,â he explained.
âA message that I wished to openly reaffirm: every human life, in whatever condition, even in the most extreme frailty, retains its inviolable dignity and deserves to be cared for, accompanied and relieved of suffering with human compassion and with the aid of the means offered by science.â
He also recalled his meeting with a group of victims of abuse, in which he asked them to help him express to other victims his wish, and that of the Church, âto listen to them and walk alongside them as they seek healing, acknowledging the pain inflicted upon their lives and working to prevent abuse.â
In Lourdes the Pope also participated in a torchlit procession and rosary, which is done every day at the Shrine. In his greetings to the Italian and German speaking faithful during the General Audience he insisted on the importance of praying the rosary for peace during this upcoming month of October.
Lastly, the Pope touched upon his visit to Metz â âa region of France and Europe ravaged by the Second World Warâ â and the third and final leg of his Journey.
He cited the figure of Robert Schuman, one of the founders of the European Union who spent much of his life in Metz and promoted peace after WWII.
âContemporary Europe was indeed born as a project for peace in the wake of the destruction wrought by war. We might say that what happened to Notre-Dame in Paris with the fire was what had happened to Europe during the Second World War,â the Pope reflected.
âAnd Europe was reborn, founded on those principles of democracy, solidarity and fraternity amongst peoples, which owe much to its Christian roots. Even today, it is on these foundations and with this vital âlifebloodâ that the European project can be renewed, in a far more globalized world.â
In this regard he also pointed to the importance of interreligious dialogue, recalling his meeting in Metz with representatives of various faiths where they signed the âMetz Appealâ for dialogue and peace.
Regarding the Second World War, in his greetings to Italian-speaking faithful, Pope Leo XIV also mentioned the beatification in Bologna last Sunday, September 27 of three martyred priests who were killed in 1944 by Nazi troops. âThe supreme sacrifice of these ministers of God shows todayâs Christians the courage to stand by their brothers and sisters, especially in times of trial,â he added.
The Pope concluded his catechesis by recalling the motto of the trip - âSo that the world may have lifeâ - and expressing the hope that his Journey might bring âabundant and lasting fruit.â
In his greetings to the Portuguese-speaking pilgrims he reiterated this idea: âMay the public witness of love for Jesus Christ that we have seen in France be an inspiration to the entire Church. Let us not hide our faith!â
In his words to the English-speaking faithful the Pope also offered âa special greeting to the seminarians from the Pontifical Irish College" and the pilgrims attending the diaconate ordination of the Pontifical North American College on October 1.

On September 9, 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported that John Ternus took the stage for the first time as Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s chief executive. He became just the third CEO since Steve Jobs returned to the company in 1997 and used his debut product launch to introduce the foldable iPhone Duo alongside a strategic decision to eliminate baseline iPhone 18 models in favor of steering buyers toward Pro and Pro Max tiers.
Ternus, a 25-year Apple veteran who led hardware engineering since 2021 and personally oversaw development of the foldable iPhone, took over from Tim Cook on September 1 after 15 years of Cook's leadership.
Don't Miss: Cook Hands Ternus Apple (AAPL) that Still has to Prove itself on AI
John Ternus brings deep product-development experience to Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) as he takes over the company. Ternus spent years running Apple's hardware engineering organization and oversaw development across the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and AirPods before becoming CEO. He now begins his tenure with Apple's first foldable iPhone and one of the company's biggest hardware redesigns in years. It gives investors a leader with direct experience managing the products that generate most of Apple's revenue.
Apple is using higher-end products and selective price increases to protect economics as memory and storage costs rise sharply. The company raised the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starting prices by $100 to $1,199 and $1,299 after surging memory costs pressured the electronics industry. Apple also chose not to refresh its base iPhone and Air models at the event, concentrating its newest hardware on premium devices that can better absorb component inflation and support stronger revenue per device.
The first major launch under Ternus shows that Apple prepared a substantive product transition rather than simply changing leadership. Ternus used his first event as CEO to introduce the $1,999 iPhone Duo, upgraded Pro models, and an AI strategy built around on-device processing and privacy. Tim Cook also moved to executive chairman instead of leaving Apple entirely. It gives Ternus access to continuity at the top while he establishes his own product strategy and pushes Apple further into AI-enabled hardware.
Look Into: Apple (AAPL)'s New CEO Bets Big on a $1,999 Foldable iPhone
Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s premium-focused launch strategy could make demand more sensitive to price. The iPhone 18 Pro now starts at $1,199, the Pro Max at $1,299, and the foldable Duo at $1,999. Apple left the base iPhone and Air without new generations at this event. Existing lower-priced models remain available. But Apple must still convince consumers that the newest hardware justifies significantly higher prices as component inflation pushes smartphones further into premium territory.
Ternus inherits Apple at a moment when the company still needs to prove that its AI strategy can match its hardware strength. Apple enters his tenure while playing catch-up in artificial intelligence, even as Ternus now positions privacy and on-device processing as key differentiators. Apple's scale gives the company enormous resources. However, the new CEO must turn Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into compelling everyday products while competitors continue investing aggressively in generative AI.
Apple also faces real supply and margin pressure as Ternus starts his tenure. The firm reported a 48.1% gross margin excluding tariff benefits in fiscal Q3 as rising memory costs weighed on profitability. Management warned that significant supply constraints could restrict product availability. Apple can raise prices to offset some of those pressures, but higher prices could eventually weaken demand, forcing Ternus to balance margins, unit growth, and supply availability during his first major product cycle as CEO.

The iPhone Duo, higher-priced Pro models and Apple's growing emphasis on on-device AI give him several ways to reinforce Apple's premium ecosystem while selective price increases help offset rising component costs. articles.content_orig:
A former Cornell University student filed a lawsuit this month alleging she was drugged and gang raped inside a fraternity house in 2024, and the fresh scrutiny has prompted local prosecutors to reopen the investigation and the state attorney general to start a review of the school’s initial response to the allegations.
The 101-page lawsuit details disturbing allegations about what the woman, identified as Jane Doe, says unfolded inside Chi Phi’s frat house the night of October 19, 2024, and how the university and local prosecutors in Ithaca, New York, handled the case. Doe is accusing seven members of the frat of participating in the assault while she was unable to consent.
The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office said Monday it reopened the case to seek a grand jury review after being “asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members.”
County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said no criminal charges were initially filed because Doe had not provided Cornell police in 2024 with the same key allegations outlined in the new lawsuit.
Doe’s attorney says the information was promptly given to Cornell authorities, and the report was “not materially different from what is contained in the (2026) complaint.”
The legal dispute, lack of criminal charges and the university’s response have prompted fierce backlash and revived concerns about how schools respond to allegations of campus sexual assault.
The office of New York Attorney General Letitia James, meanwhile, is reviewing Cornell University’s response to the rape allegations, a spokesperson for the office said Tuesday.
The complaint names more than a dozen defendants, including the seven fraternity members from 2024, Cornell University and the Chi Phi fraternity. Allegations include negligence, breach of contract, sexual assault and battery, and violations of New York’s Human Rights Law.
CNN has sought comment from several named parties in the lawsuit.
The complaint says Doe was 20 and had been drinking at her sorority house and a bar before she arrived at the Chi Phi house to visit a friend, who was one of the fraternity members, on the night of October 19, 2024.
According to the suit, Doe had already consumed about 10 standard drinks within the previous three hours when she arrived at the fraternity house.
The complaint alleges the friend and another fraternity member gave her more alcohol and pressured her into snorting a substance they described as ketamine, and that she was then sexually assaulted while “incapable of consent.” A third fraternity member eventually entered the room and also sexually assaulted her, the complaint alleges.
At roughly 1:42 a.m., one of the men allegedly sent a message to the fraternity’s Snapchat group chat a message – titled “Chi Phi Actives” – stating there was “free p*ssy” upstairs.
By doing this, the suit alleges, one of the accused “encouraged other … chapter members to join in on the gang rape of plaintiff.”
A photo of a portion of the chat is included in the filing. Multiple fraternity members then entered the room, where one of the newcomers kissed her without her consent, and one of the first three men commanded her to take more ketamine and groped her, according to the complaint.
The seven defendants in the complaint poured ketamine onto her body and snorted it, the complaint says.
Eventually, five defendants left the room, and the remaining two men led her to a different room, where those two instructed her to take more ketamine and sexually assaulted her until about 5:45 a.m., the complaint says.
An attorney for one of the accused fraternity brothers denied any wrongdoing by his client.
“Even the district attorney’s office, led by a chief prosecutor with the duty to pursue justice and uphold the rule of law without bias or favor, filed no charges against (him) because what she alleged did not happen,” attorney Jeremy Saland said in a statement to CNN. He said his client “never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way.”
An attorney for a different student gave ABC News a statement acknowledging that student participated in the Snapchat conversation mentioned in the complaint but denying that he engaged in sexual activity.
“I did not participate in any sexual activity or drug use. I was not found responsible by Cornell for any of the accusations involving sexual activity and drug use for which others received serious consequences,” the student said through his attorney. “I thoughtlessly engaged in Snapchat and briefly stopped in the room where misconduct happened but not when it happened.”
CNN is working to determine whether the other fraternity brothers have representation.
Chi Phi declined to discuss the specific allegations, citing pending litigation, but said it “unequivocally condemns sexual violence.”
“Our founding principles of Truth, Honor, and Personal Integrity, and our mission of Building Better Men, call on every brother to demonstrate character through his actions and respect for the dignity and safety of others,” the national fraternity said in a release. “Sexual violence is fundamentally incompatible with those expectations.”
The district attorney said the report Jane Doe made to university police differs significantly from the allegations in the lawsuit.
Nothing in Doe’s original statement indicated she was drugged without consent or had sex against her will, Van Houten said. According to the accuser’s statement, “each time Jane Doe asked to stop the sexual conduct, the sexual conduct stopped.”
Van Houten’s office has not released the full police report. CNN has asked Doe’s attorney for a response to Van Houten’s statement and for a copy of her complete 2024 police statement.
During a contentious interview Monday, CNN’s Jake Tapper pressed Van Houten on why there wasn’t a more expansive investigation from law enforcement or the DA’s office after the report was made in 2024.
“We can’t change what happened in the past as much as the community is outraged,” Van Houten said. “My job under the New York State Constitution is to apply the penal law of New York state. We are constrained by that law. Whether you agree with it, whether you think someone’s conduct is morally repugnant or vulgar or disgusting. I’m still constrained by the law.”
The district attorney doubled down on that argument Tuesday.
“Jane Doe told us through her six-page written statement (in 2024) what happened,” Van Houten told CNN’s Pamela Brown. “When you know that very detailed, comprehensive account does not establish a crime, it’s not ethical for a prosecutor or for the police to go out and look for or cross-examine her to find evidence of a crime.”
Van Houten on Monday acknowledged that the text message screenshots between the men “were completely vulgar and disgusting, but they had nothing to do with her consent.”
Tapper asked when Van Houten got copies of the text messages, included in the complaint, that the fraternity brothers sent each other.
Van Houten said that his team did not see the text messages evidence initially.
“They were not part of our initial analysis, but I understand that Cornell had them, and they sent them to our team,” he said.
The Cornell University Police Department sent the DA’s office the Snapchat screenshot in November 2024, school officials said Tuesday.
Earlier, Doe’s attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra, said in a release that he believes the initial investigation was inadequate.
“It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint,” Giuffra said.

articles.title_zh: ‘No way they can beat us’: Rutte rebuffs Russian nuclear threats to NATO
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday issued a strong rebuke to Russia after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening nuclear escalation over NATO activity near its border.
"We had to reply and make clear to [Russia] that NATO is a defensive alliance ... and stop the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats because it's not helpful," Rutte said at a security summit in Brussels. "NATO is so much stronger than Russia is, so there's no way they can ever beat us."
"The best way to deal with this is to have a little bit of calm," he added. "That's the message: calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going — that's how we deal with it."
Rutte's unusually strong remarks underscore the growing tensions between Moscow and NATO countries as hybrid attacks and Russian-linked sabotage proliferate across Europe.
In recent days, Russia's embassy in Belgium sent NATO a note alleging the alliance was displaying "reckless and irresponsible" behavior near its Kaliningrad exclave, following alliance exercises involving several reconnaissance planes, ground forces and fighter jets near the region, which is between Poland and Lithuania, last month.
"We have emphasised that Russia possesses the necessary means to repel any potential aggression and is prepared to deploy its entire arsenal to defend its territory should NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country," the embassy wrote on social media.
In its letter to NATO, Moscow explicitly mentions the use of its nuclear arsenal and issues specific threats to hit allied territory, according to one NATO diplomat briefed on the letter, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.
NATO has sent a note back to Russian officials in response, the alliance's spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed.
"We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia," she said in a statement. "We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Inside NATO, some allies are dismissing the threat. "Our reading is that they want to intimidate allied public opinion so that allies stop supporting [Ukraine], while, at the same time, presenting NATO as the one that would be responsible for an eventual escalation," said the same NATO diplomat cited above. "Textbook Russian propaganda."
"Russia always accelerates when it's the most guilty or when [it] loses," said a second alliance diplomat. "So they are cornered now and they transfer the blame on NATO."
Russia's embassy to Belgium didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Instagram announced on Wednesday that it’s bringing an AI video assistant tool to Edits , its CapCut competitor.
This conversational AI chatbot is intended to provide personalized feedback to creators, rather than generic advice.
“The assistant knows your account’s Instagram metrics, things like follows, views, video retention, likes, shares and combines them with your comments, what’s trending on Instagram and what your audience is into,” Brett Westervelt, who leads the Edits app, said. “It can spot patterns in your performance over time and surface actionable insights that are hard to see from the metrics alone.”
Westervelt added that Edits worked closely with a group of creators in developing the tool.
“One thing we heard consistently: creators want a tool that handles the analysis, not one that does the creative work for them,” he wrote. “Edits assistant does the digging for you. The creative calls are still yours.”
Meta first previewed the Edits AI assistant in June at an invite-only creator event, where it also said it was working on an Edits desktop app. It’s not the only company working on tools like this, though. YouTube announced last week that it is also working on a conversational video editing tool , which should be available early next year.
From what we can tell so far, it looks like Meta is taking a more analytics-driven approach with its AI assistant than YouTube, which suggested creators would use its AI to help with the actual editing process.
Creators will have a limit to how much they can use the AI tool, but they can unlock more usage with a Meta One subscription.

Apple ( AAPL ) stock rose in early trading on Wednesday following a report that the company is preparing to host an event next month outlining its entry into the smart home space.
According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman , Apple will unveil an all-new smart home hub designed to control devices throughout the home, serve as a digital calendar and reminder list, play music, make video calls, and more.
Shares of Apple rose nearly 3%.
The hub, which can be mounted on a wall or placed on a counter with an accompanying stand, is designed to recognize users and provide them with personalized content via voice or facial recognition. It will also take advantage of Apple's new Siri AI platform, which it launched in beta earlier this month.
Apple is also working on a secondary version of the smart home hub featuring a robotic arm that lets the screen rotate 360 degrees.
The home hub would stand as the first new product category for Apple under CEO John Ternus , though the project has been in the works for some time. It could also serve as a lucrative new revenue stream for the company if it catches on.
Current do-it-yourself hub-style solutions require users to mount iPads to their walls to control smart home products or access them via their iPhones.
In addition to the hub, Apple is also rolling out new versions of its Apple TV set-top box and HomePod mini smart speaker. Both devices will look roughly the same as their existing versions, though they'll get more powerful processors to run Siri AI.
According to Gurman , Apple is looking to speed up its product development by making the company leaner via layoffs and other reductions.
Apple is entering a market traditionally dominated by Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), which had early success in the smart home space thanks to their Alexa and Google Assistant platforms, respectively.
The company's home offerings fall under its Wearables, Home, and Accessories segment, which brought in $35.68 billion in 2025, making it Apple's third-largest segment behind the iPhone and Services.
The iPhone, however, is still by far the company's most important product, bringing in $209.58 billion of Apple's $416.16 billion in total revenue last year.
